opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
body:
Yesterday I had an encounter with a potential client who has stayed with me far longer than our conversation itself.

She talked a lot — animated, passionate, intelligent, and clearly someone who had lived several lifetimes despite her young age. She spoke openly about society, people in power, the workers building her home, personal growth, mental health, spirituality, and the long road she had traveled to become more fully herself. She made one thing clear early on: she was spiritual, but not religious. She wanted that distinction understood.

I liked her immediately. Her honesty. Her charisma. Her confidence. She had given herself permission to become who she was without allowing the world to completely consume her. I admired that.

But I left unsettled. Not because of who she was. Because of who I was in that moment.

I listened while she spoke. I responded occasionally. I made passing references to the soul when she described the inner work she had done. But I kept finding myself asking afterward: did I witness her, but fail to witness to her?

I thought about God many times during that conversation. I thought about how much He has carried me, how deeply I believe that we are loved, known, and called into something larger than ourselves. I thought about asking her what “spiritual but not religious” actually meant to her. I wondered who God was to her. I wondered why religion became a boundary. Yet I stayed mostly quiet.

And now I find myself bothered by that. Not because I think every conversation should become evangelization. But because I do not want to become ashamed of what I love most.

So much has happened culturally that people often label each other before they know one another. Once labeled, dialogue becomes predictable. Curiosity disappears. People assume they already know who God is, who religion is, and who believers are, and they stop listening before the relationship even begins.

Today I read 2 Timothy: “Be persistent whether convenient or inconvenient… For the time will come when people will not tolerate sound doctrine but, following their own desires and insatiable curiosity, will accumulate teachers…”

And I wondered if that time is already here.

Then another thought came. Maybe persistence is not always speaking louder. Maybe persistence sometimes looks like staying available longer.

Looking back, I think the missed opportunity was not that I failed to proclaim Christ. It was that I failed to ask more questions. What made spirituality feel safer than religion? What sustained her through those many lifetimes she feels she has lived? When she speaks about the inner self, what does she believe that self actually is?

Questions open doors.

And perhaps this is what I am learning: God does not always ask me to command the ship. Sometimes He asks me to stay present on it.

I still wish I had asked more. But I also realize this: I have thought about this woman long after the conversation ended. I remembered her wounds, her searching, her language for meaning. That means I was listening.

And maybe next time, listening becomes curiosity, curiosity becomes relationship, and relationship becomes the place where people feel safe enough to speak honestly about who God is, who they believe Him to be, or why they believe He is absent altogether. Because people are rarely argued into God. More often, they are invited toward Him.
